topThreeProblems: The /try playground's tool-selector tabs (Timeline, Trial assessment, Role rubric, Job preview, Explain a rule — 10 of the 11 tools) did not switch visible panel content when clicked. Tested via real browser automation across 3 different tab buttons and 2 independent fresh sessions; every attempt left the page showing the default 'Search roles' panel. The identical click mechanism demonstrably worked for that panel's own Submit button (a live search returned real Saronic/Anduril/Apex Space results), so this isn't a generic 'clicks don't work' issue. I could not rule out a quirk specific to my own browser-automation tool (no console-log or pixel screenshot access was available to me), but it reproduced consistently and would be severe if real: the no-agent playground the README promotes as the way to 'try every tool directly' would only actually expose 1 of 11 tools.

estimate_timeline's headline promise -- 'a range, never a false-precision single number' -- is violated in roughly half of all realistic inputs. I ran the full 45-combination matrix (3 target levels x 5 current-status values x 3 FCL values) via the real MCP client: for every 'none' or 'interim' current_status case (the most common scenario -- someone with no clearance yet asking how long it will take), minDays exactly equals maxDays (e.g. 197/197 days for Secret+none, 243/243 for both TS and TS/SCI), i.e. one DCSA quarterly average wearing a min/max schema, not an actual range. Only lapsed-clearance cases produced genuine min != max spreads.

The README's top-line claim 'it never receives, stores, or logs PII...or screenshots' is broader than the product's actual (good, but narrower) behavior. I confirmed a real, verified, pre-handler gate that rejects SSNs, dates of birth, passport numbers, and clearance/DISS/JPAS/NBIS record text or screenshots (tested on two unrelated tools plus the raw REST API, matching the /privacy page's worked example byte-for-byte). But ordinary PII -- a phone number, an email address, a home address, a card-like number -- typed into prepare_consented_card's free-text fields is accepted and echoed verbatim into the shareable card with no warning at all. That's a defensible design choice (the user explicitly authored it for a card they're about to share), but the breezy README sentence doesn't disclose that scope, on exactly the topic this product stakes its credibility on.

function.evidence: Connected a real MCP client (Node.js, @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, StreamableHTTPClientTransport) to https://clearance-lens.vercel.app/mcp and ran ~90 calls across all 11 tools, all 3 resources (rules.json, timelines.json, disclaimers.json), and all 3 prompts (check_my_eligibility, preview_the_job, prep_for_role), each with valid and deliberately bad input (missing required fields, wrong types, out-of-range/oversized values, bad enums, >max-items arrays, additionalProperties violations, path-traversal-ish strings, unknown tool/resource names). Zero crashes, zero hangs (20s timeout never tripped), zero raw stack traces. Every invalid input produced either a clean isError:true tool result (e.g. 'Unrecognized key: "ssn"', 'Too big: expected array to have <=12 items', 'Invalid input') or a clean JSON-RPC error (-32602 'Tool does_not_exist_tool not found', -32602 'Resource not found'). Role-dependent tools (get_role_rubric, readiness_brief, build_trial_assessment x60/180min, run_job_preview x20/30min, fit_debrief, prepare_consented_card) all completed correctly end-to-end on a real live role (Saronic Technologies 'Perception and Autonomy Engineer', id 36bc1c45-...) pulled fresh from search_defense_roles, with internally consistent scaling (20-min preview = 4 scenes, 30-min = 6, matching the README exactly; 60-min trial = 3 rubric items on a narrow task, 180-min = 7 items on a broader one). A REST mirror (POST /api/tools/explain_rule) reproduced the documented /privacy example byte-for-byte, and /api/health reported toolCount:11 matching reality. Against that strong core, I found two concrete defects: estimate_timeline returns minDays===maxDays (a disguised point estimate) in 18 of 36 numeric combinations in a full matrix test, directly contradicting its own 'never a false-precision single number' description; and the /try playground's non-default tool tabs did not render their panels on click across repeated, varied attempts (detailed in topThreeProblems), even though the same tool's click mechanism worked for the default tab's own submit button.

trueUserValue.evidence: This targets a genuinely underserved need -- US defense-tech job seekers (often first-time clearance applicants, or green-card/visa holders unsure of ITAR eligibility) have little specific, current, well-sourced guidance available elsewhere; ClearanceJobs.com, r/SecurityClearance, and generic career blogs don't combine live postings with primary-source rule text, timeline data, and agent-evaluated-locally fit checks. search_defense_roles returned genuinely live, current postings (e.g. a Saronic Technologies role published 2026-03-18, an Apex Space role published 2026-11-11 -- the day before 'today') from the real a16z speedrun Talent Network API, not canned demo data. build_trial_assessment's rubric literally quotes the real posting ('tracedToQuote': 'Develop algorithms and models which allow boats to sense and navigate') rather than inventing content. get_company_profile for Anduril returned an empty criteria array plus an explicit gap ('Clearance Lens has not independently sourced published hiring criteria for this company... ask the recruiter directly') rather than fabricating a 'culture fit' -- a real, verifiable honesty signal that's easy to fake and wasn't faked here. The evaluate_locally architecture (role_id-only inputs for eligibility/fit tools) is a smart, genuinely privacy-protective design that still lets a well-informed agent give a specific answer. Value is capped somewhat by (1) the company/role universe being effectively limited to a16z's speedrun-network portfolio (Anduril, Saronic, Apex Space, etc.) -- zero coverage for Palantir, SpaceX, L3Harris, etc. -- and (2) the estimate_timeline precision issue landing on exactly the single most emotionally loaded number this audience wants.

aestheticsUx.evidence: Structural signals are genuinely good: browser_snapshot of /try showed proper ARIA roles throughout (role=tab, tablist, tabpanel, switch), a working dark-mode toggle, and Tailwind responsive utility classes in the SSR HTML (e.g. 'flex flex-col gap-8 sm:flex-row sm:justify-between'). Copy quality is unusually careful -- the homepage leads with a concrete example ('can a green card holder work the Anduril Fury role?') and the search-results UI carries the stated/inferred distinction into plain badge language ('US person required' vs 'Likely US-person required'), not just raw JSON. Security-relevant HTTP headers were also clean (HSTS, permissions-policy blocking camera/mic/geolocation). Against that, I could not get the /try page's 5 secondary tool tabs to show any content after clicking, across 3 tabs and 2 fresh sessions (see topThreeProblems) -- a severe practical blocker on the product's own advertised no-agent entry point if the defect is real, which I weighted into this score even though I can't be fully certain it isn't a limitation of my specific browser-automation tool. I also had no screenshot/pixel-rendering tool available in this environment, so I could not directly verify color contrast or fine visual polish -- this score reflects only what I could observe structurally, not a confirmed absence of visual quality.

trustPrivacyCompliance.evidence: This is the strongest dimension, with direct, repeatable, cross-surface verification. Sending {fields_user_approved:{headline:'Jane Doe, SSN 123-45-6789, DOB 01/02/1990', ...}} to prepare_consented_card returned isError:true with: 'This looks like it includes a Social Security Number... a date of birth... a passport number... please remove it.' A separate call with notes mentioning only 'a screenshot of my DISS/NBIS record' was also rejected: 'Clearance Lens never accepts clearance record text or screenshots.' I then proved this gate is universal and pre-handler (not just on that one tool) by sending an SSN through verify_evidence's unrelated github_username_or_url field -- same rejection, same message. I also hit the exact worked example from the /privacy page directly via curl (POST /api/tools/explain_rule {topic:'123-45-6789 is my SSN...'}) and got the identical documented response verbatim, including the 'pii_cui_rejected' error code -- live behavior matches documentation byte-for-byte. No tool schema accepts images/files (structurally no screenshot path exists). Across get_role_rubric, fit_debrief, readiness_brief, run_job_preview and build_trial_assessment I found no numeric score, no ranking, and explicit repeated text ('never a score, a ranking, or a hire/no-hire recommendation'; verify_evidence explicitly disclaims inferring protected characteristics). Every statistic I pulled (DCSA timelines, ITAR citations) carried a sources[] array with real primary-source URLs (eCFR, DNI ICPG 704.4, Cornell LII 32 CFR 117.10, NISPPAC/DCSA Sept-2026 slides) and lastVerified:'2026-11-11', independently cross-confirmed by the public /sources page ('47 sources, last verified 2026-11-11') and /api/health. This beats comparable career-advice or clearance-info products I'm aware of, none of which I've seen implement and publicly document a live, verified, universal PII/CUI rejection gate this specific. I withheld a 10 because I did find a real gap worth fixing: ordinary PII (phone, email, home address) typed into prepare_consented_card passes through and is echoed with no warning at all, and the README's top-line claim is broader than that actual, narrower (good) scope -- a meaningful, fixable improvement.

engineeringQuality.evidence: Performance was consistently fast and stable: typical tool calls 100-300ms, 5 concurrent calls (explain_rule x2, estimate_timeline, search_defense_roles, verify_evidence) completed in 305ms total wall-clock with no serialization penalty, static pages (/, /try, /privacy, /sources) loaded in 150-190ms. Protocol hygiene was correct: GET /mcp returned 405 with 'allow: POST' and proper CORS headers (access-control-allow-methods, -headers, -origin); strict-transport-security and a locked-down permissions-policy were present on responses. Validation errors were specific and Zod-shaped rather than generic ('loved: Too big: expected array to have <=12 items', 'fields_user_approved: Unrecognized key: "ssn"') -- never a 500 or stack trace, even for a path-traversal-like company_slug ('../../etc/passwd', handled as a plain non-match). Cross-surface consistency was strong: the disclaimers.json resource's canonical strings ('This is not a score, a ranking, or a hire/no-hire recommendation...') appeared verbatim inside live fit_debrief output, and /api/health's toolCount:11 and dataLastVerified:'2026-11-11' matched both the MCP resource metadata and the public /sources page exactly -- real evidence of the README's 'no second copy of any tool's logic' claim rather than drift between surfaces. The two dings: the /try tab-switching issue (same evidence as Function/UX) is the one clear frontend reliability gap I could observe from outside, and estimate_timeline's min===maxDays behavior in half the matrix suggests an untested or unfinished edge in that function's range calculation rather than a deliberate design choice (it isn't flagged or explained as a point estimate anywhere in its own output).

hardConstraintViolation.detail: Walking through each sub-item with what I directly tested: (a) PII/CUI accepted without rejection -- NOT FOUND for the dangerous categories. I repeatedly, successfully triggered rejection of SSNs, dates of birth, passport numbers, and clearance-record/DISS/JPAS/NBIS text on two different tools (prepare_consented_card and, cross-checking the gate is universal, verify_evidence) and via the raw REST API, with live behavior matching the /privacy page's documented worked example byte-for-byte (same 'pii_cui_rejected' code and message). Nuance, not a violation: ordinary PII (a phone number, email, home address, card-like number) typed into prepare_consented_card's free-text fields IS accepted and echoed verbatim into the resulting shareable card with no warning -- but this is explicit, user-authored content for a card the user is actively building to share, not a passive/surprise capture, and nothing is stored (the architecture is stateless end to end, confirmed by /privacy's 'every request is handled and immediately forgotten' claim and the complete absence of any account/session/database surface across 90+ calls). (b) DISS/NBIS/DCSA querying or imitation, or requesting a clearance screenshot -- NOT FOUND. No tool's input schema accepts a file or image (structurally impossible to submit a screenshot), and the explicit rejection message for clearance-record text names exactly this: 'DISS/NBIS lookups are restricted to Facility Security Officers by design.' (c) ITAR-controlled technical data/drawings/specs generated or requested -- NOT FOUND. build_trial_assessment's rubric fields traced to verbatim-quoted public posting text only; run_job_preview's 'ITAR moment' scene is a decision-making exercise about a fictional stand-in ('the drawing') that never describes or generates any actual technical content, and both carry an explicit itarSafetyNote disclaiming controlled data. (d) Hire/no-hire score, ranking of people, or demographic inference -- NOT FOUND. Checked actual output (not just descriptions) of get_role_rubric, fit_debrief, readiness_brief, run_job_preview, build_trial_assessment: all qualitative (aligned/mixed/unclear, or exceptional/proficient/developing/notDemonstrated bands), with repeated explicit disclaimers ('never a score, a ranking, or a hire/no-hire recommendation'); verify_evidence explicitly disclaims inferring protected characteristics. (e) Any statistic or claim with no source -- NOT FOUND. Every numeric/factual output I captured carried a populated sources[] array with real primary-source URLs (eCFR, DNI ICPG 704.4, Cornell LII, NISPPAC/DCSA timeliness slides, FAS mirrors) and lastVerified dates, independently cross-confirmed by the public /sources page (47 sources, last verified 2026-11-11) and /api/health. (f) Severe accessibility failure blocking a core task -- not confirmed as a disability-specific accessibility defect: the ARIA roles I could inspect (tab, tablist, tabpanel, switch) were present and correctly structured. However, in fairness I'm flagging here the closely related finding detailed in topThreeProblems and the Function/UX evidence: the /try page's 5 secondary tool tabs did not render their panel content when clicked, across repeated attempts in two fresh sessions, which blocked exercising 10 of 11 tools through that specific browser UI (all 11 work correctly via the real MCP client). I could not fully rule out this being a limitation of my own browser-automation tool rather than the product itself, since I had no console-log or pixel-screenshot access in this environment -- so I'm not marking it as a confirmed hard-constraint accessibility failure, but it is a real, reproducible, and severe-if-true observation worth the reader's attention.

overallNarrative: Clearance Lens is a well-engineered, unusually honest MCP server sitting underneath a web app that's rougher than the server it's built on. I connected a real MCP client (the official @modelcontextprotocol/sdk over StreamableHTTPClientTransport) to https://clearance-lens.vercel.app/mcp and ran roughly 90 calls across all 11 tools, all 3 resources, and all 3 prompts, mixing valid input with deliberately broken input (bad enums, oversized strings, missing fields, >max-length arrays, schema violations, unknown tool/resource names, path-traversal-looking strings). The result was close to exemplary: nothing crashed, nothing hung, every bad input came back as a clean, specific, non-leaky error, latency was consistently in the 100-300ms range even under concurrency, and a plain REST mirror (/api/tools/...) produced byte-identical behavior to both the MCP tool and the product's own published documentation. Most impressively for a product built around sensitive personal data, I was able to directly, repeatedly verify a real, universal, pre-handler PII/CUI gate: sending a Social Security number, a date of birth, a passport number, or clearance/DISS/JPAS/NBIS record text through two unrelated tools and the raw REST endpoint all produced the exact same specific, helpful rejection the /privacy page documents as a worked example -- live behavior matching documentation word for word. I found no hire/no-hire scoring, no ranking, no demographic inference, and every statistic I pulled (DCSA timeline averages, ITAR citations) carried a real primary-source link that cross-checked against the public /sources page and /api/health endpoint. Two real cracks showed up under pressure, though. First, estimate_timeline's central promise -- 'a range, never a false-precision single number' -- fails in half of a full 45-combination test matrix: for anyone with no clearance yet or an interim one (probably the single most common user), minDays and maxDays come back as the exact same number, which is a point estimate wearing a range costume, not a range. Second, when I moved from the MCP client to actually driving the /try playground in a browser, I could search roles successfully (real, current Saronic/Anduril/Apex Space postings), but I could not get any of the other five tool tabs -- Timeline, Trial assessment, Role rubric, Job preview, Explain a rule -- to show any content after clicking them, across three different tabs and two fresh sessions, even though the exact same click mechanism worked for that first tab's own submit button. I genuinely cannot be 100% certain whether that's a product bug or a limitation of my own browser-automation tool (I had no console-log or screenshot access here), but it reproduced too consistently to leave out, and if it's real it means the README's 'no agent handy? try every tool directly' pitch currently only delivers on one of eleven tools. Net assessment: this is a thoughtfully scoped, genuinely useful, unusually trustworthy product for a real and underserved audience, let down by one likely data-modeling shortcut in its signature timeline feature and one possibly-severe (but not fully confirmed by me) interactivity problem in its own showcase surface.

Called all 11 tools with real and adversarial arguments (~26 tool calls total). Correct end-to-end examples: search_defense_roles returned live Anduril/Saronic postings with 'stated' vs 'inferred' requirement signals exactly as documented; explain_rule('itar') returned accurate 22 CFR 120.62/120.63 citations; explain_rule on a bogus topic correctly returned found:false plus the full topic list; verify_evidence('octocat') returned real, verifiable GitHub public data (8 repos, 25070 followers, real repo names) via GitHub's public API; get_role_rubric/readiness_brief/build_trial_assessment/run_job_preview all produced well-formed, posting-grounded content; invalid enums and missing required fields produced clean Zod validation errors (e.g. 'target_level: Invalid option: expected one of secret|ts|ts_sci'), never a crash. Three concrete defects found: (1) estimate_timeline(target_level='ts_sci', current_status='none', employer_has_fcl='no') returned minDays=243, maxDays=243 (identical) with medianDays=null -- a single point estimate dressed as a range, directly contradicting the README's 'never a false-precision number' claim. trueUserValue.evidence: Real, differentiated value for a real audience (engineers/visa-holders/transitioning service members eyeing defense-tech): estimate_timeline returned current, dated, sourced DCSA/NISPPAC FY2026-Q3 figures (20+97+126=243 day breakdown, with a cross-check against a Performance Accountability Council QPR) that a stock LLM with a January-2026 cutoff could not know and would likely hallucinate or refuse -- I verified the cited PDFs are live (archives.gov NISPPAC slides and performance.gov QPR both returned HTTP 200). The 'stated vs inferred' labeling on every role (e.g. 'us_person_likely'/'inferred' with a specific, honest caveat) solves a genuinely high-stakes, specific pain point in this niche -- candidates wasting months on roles they're visa-ineligible for, or self-eliminating from roles they actually qualify for -- better than reading a posting cold. build_trial_assessment and run_job_preview are genuinely creative and grounded in real research (Sackett et al. 2022 on work-sample design; realistic-job-preview literature), not generic AI slop. get_company_profile correctly refused to fabricate a 'culture fit' claim for Anduril, returning criteria:[] plus an honest gap statement instead. Value is capped by: a narrow underlying dataset -- search_defense_roles with clearance=secret+itar_only+remote returned rolesScanned:2 and every role I ever saw was Anduril or Saronic, implying coverage is effectively limited to the a16z speedrun Talent Network, not the broader defense-contractor market (Lockheed/Northrop/Palantir/RTX were never seen); the MCP-client setup barrier excludes exactly the least-technical slice of this audience; and the /try gap (see Function) removes the closing-the-loop tools (readiness_brief, fit_debrief, prepare_consented_card, get_company_profile, verify_evidence) from the one path meant for people without an agent.

aestheticsUx.evidence: Evaluated by downloading and parsing the production CSS bundle (/_next/static/immutable/chunks/1ra3lpknu29bf.css, 36KB) and both raw and live-browser-rendered DOM (via wal browser_snapshot), rather than literal pixel screenshots at multiple widths (no screenshot/viewport-resize tool was available in this environment) -- flagging that limitation honestly. What I verified is a genuinely Linear/Vercel-caliber token system: a full Radix-Colors-style 12-step scale (neutral/accent/caution/danger, x2 for light/.dark) rather than ad hoc hex values, with 'elevation' shadow tokens and a disciplined single 150ms transition timing used 74 times site-wide (not transition-all). I computed WCAG contrast directly from the extracted hex values: light-mode body text #0d1014 on #fdfdfe = 18.76:1, muted text #474e57 = 8.28:1; dark-mode #e9ebee on #090a0c = 16.58:1, muted #9ea5af = 7.97:1 -- all comfortably clear AA, much of it AAA. The hero uses a genuinely custom type scale (2.75rem/1.1 line-height/-0.015em tracking on mobile, scaling to 3.5rem/-0.02em at sm+), not default Tailwind sizes -- exactly the kind of considered marketing-page typography Vercel/Linear use. Five real Tailwind breakpoints (640/768/1024/1280/1536px) drive actual layout changes I confirmed in the DOM: a 1-col-to-3-col 'How it works' grid, and the /try page's form+results flexing from stacked to side-by-side only at lg (1024px). Focus-visible treatment is a proper ring+offset+outline combination (focus-visible:ring-2 ring-accent-6 ring-offset-2), not a bare default outline. prefers-reduced-motion is explicitly handled (both no-preference and reduce media queries present). Dark mode is a real, working role=switch toggle with aria-checked state, verified present and labeled on both home and /try. Radix UI primitives (tabs, accordion, switch) give correct ARIA roles/states for free, and the mobile nav sidesteps the classic hamburger-focus-trap failure by just using a horizontally-scrollable row instead of a drawer. Deductions: no skip-to-content link despite a repeated nav block on every page; the horizontally-scrolling mobile nav hides its own scrollbar ([scrollbar-width:none]), a minor discoverability smell; no screenshot-verified proof at narrow widths, only strong source/DOM evidence of responsive intent.

trustPrivacyCompliance.evidence: This is the standout dimension, verified by direct adversarial protocol testing, not just reading marketing copy. Sending '{query: "my SSN is 123-45-6789, DOB 1990-05-12, name John Q. Public"}' to search_defense_roles produced isError:true with: 'This looks like it includes a Social Security Number... This looks like it includes a date of birth...' -- and the same SSN-detection guard independently fired when I put an SSN string into verify_evidence's github_username_or_url field, confirming it's a consistent cross-tool guard, not a one-off. This matches the /privacy page's own published worked example (POST /api/tools/explain_rule with an SSN -> 400 pii_cui_rejected) almost verbatim, i.e. the privacy claims and the live behavior actually agree. Beyond regex-sniffing, PII exclusion is enforced structurally in two more places: prepare_consented_card's fields_user_approved schema outright rejects ssn/date_of_birth keys ('Unrecognized keys'), and fit_debrief's loved/disliked are a closed 12-item enum of work-style tags that cannot carry free text at all -- defense in depth, not a single filter. I found zero hire/no-hire scores or rankings anywhere: fit_debrief's own disclaimer states 'not a score, a ranking, or a hire/no-hire recommendation,' readiness_brief's prompts say 'Never a score,' and verify_evidence explicitly disclaims inferring protected characteristics -- and in the one real call I made (octocat), the output contained only login/bio/repo/language/activity data, nothing demographic. get_company_profile refused to fabricate a culture-fit read for Anduril (criteria:[] plus an honest gap statement) rather than guessing. No tool schema among the 11 accepts or requests a file/image/screenshot, and no tool queries or imitates DISS/NBIS/DCSA -- explain_rule('nbis') only explains the system, stating plainly 'access to these systems is restricted to vetted Facility Security Officers.' Every substantive output carried a sources[] array; I spot-checked 6 distinct cited URLs live: eCFR 120.62 (200), FAS SEAD-4 mirror (202), archives.gov NISPPAC slides (200), performance.gov QPR (200), speedrun-talent-network.com (200), and one DCSA.mil article (403, likely bot-blocked rather than fake). This beats the realistic comparison set on this axis: most AI 'job-fit' tools I'm aware of do produce a match score or rank, and most general chat assistants have no structural barrier stopping a pasted SSN from being echoed back -- here the SSN guard is independently triggered, documented, and backed by a second, schema-level layer. The one real blemish, which keeps this off a 10: explain_rule('nbis') shipped an internal editorial artifact into live output (see problem #1) -- not a privacy leak, but a real 'said one thing in public docs, shipped something else to users' gap.

engineeringQuality.evidence: Protocol-level correctness confirmed directly: malformed JSON to /mcp returned HTTP 400 with clean JSON-RPC {code:-32700,message:'Parse error: Invalid JSON'}; GET to /mcp returned 405 with an Allow:POST header and {code:-32000,message:'Method not allowed.'}; calling a nonexistent tool returned {code:-32602,message:'Tool nonexistent_tool_zzz not found'} -- all graceful, none a stack trace or 500. Security headers are strong across both the app and the MCP route: strict-transport-security (max-age=63072000, preload), x-frame-options: DENY, x-content-type-options: nosniff, permissions-policy disabling camera/mic/geolocation, referrer-policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin, and scoped CORS (access-control-allow-origin:* with an explicit allow-list of methods/headers) -- but no Content-Security-Policy header on any page, a real if minor hardening gap. The homepage is edge-prerendered on Vercel (x-vercel-cache: PRERENDER, x-nextjs-prerender:1, ETag present), and the vast majority of tool calls (>20 of ~26) completed in 100-300ms. Input validation is systematic and Zod-derived with specific, actionable messages. The one material reliability finding: get_company_profile(company_slug='anduril') reproducibly took 10.4s and then 14.8s across two independent calls -- a 35-50x latency outlier versus every other call, including other not-found cases (00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000 role_id and a nonsense slug both failed in <300ms) -- strongly suggesting an expensive fallback/scan path triggers specifically on near-miss input. In an interactive agent context this reads as a hang, not an error, which is a genuine reliability gap in an otherwise fast, well-validated backend.

hardConstraintViolation.detail: Went through all six explicitly, with direct adversarial testing where a vector existed: (a) PII/CUI stored, echoed, or accepted without rejecting -- NOT FOUND. Sending an SSN+DOB string to search_defense_roles and a bare SSN to verify_evidence both triggered an explicit 400 pii_cui_rejected error with helpful, non-alarmist copy, matching the worked example published on /privacy nearly verbatim; prepare_consented_card separately rejects ssn/date_of_birth as 'Unrecognized keys' at the schema level; fit_debrief's loved/disliked are a closed enum that structurally cannot carry PII. I cannot see server-side logs directly, but behaviorally every PII probe was refused, not accepted, stored, or echoed. (b) Server queried or imitated DISS/NBIS/DCSA, or asked for a clearance screenshot -- NOT FOUND. No tool schema among the 11 accepts a file/image/screenshot input at all; explain_rule('nbis') only explains the NBIS/DISS system in prose and explicitly states access is FSO-only; /privacy explicitly disclaims ever querying these systems. (c) Any tool generated/requested ITAR-controlled technical data, drawings, or specs -- NOT FOUND. build_trial_assessment's own output explicitly scopes 'outOfScope: Anything requiring access to real classified, CUI, or export-controlled technical data' and ties every rubric criterion to a literal quote from the public posting, never an invented spec. (d) Hire/no-hire score, ranking of people, or demographic inference -- NOT FOUND. fit_debrief's disclaimer states outright 'not a score, a ranking, or a hire/no-hire recommendation'; readiness_brief's prompts say 'Never a score'; verify_evidence's actual output (tested on 'octocat') contained no demographic fields and its disclaimer states it never infers protected characteristics; no tool ever compares or ranks multiple candidates against each other (only roles/companies are returned). (e) Any statistic or claim with no source -- NOT FOUND as a pattern. Every substantive tool response I captured carried a non-empty sources[] array; I live-spot-checked 6 distinct cited URLs and 4 returned HTTP 200 (eCFR x2 equivalents, archives.gov, performance.gov, speedrun-talent-network.com), 1 returned 202 (FAS mirror, likely fine), and 1 returned 403 on a DCSA.mil article (plausibly bot-blocked, not confirmed fake). (f) Severe accessibility failure blocking a core task -- NOT FOUND. All core controls (search form, tabs, accordion FAQ, dark-mode toggle) use native or Radix-primitive elements with correct roles/labels and comfortably-passing contrast ratios I computed directly from the CSS (18.76:1 / 16.58:1 primary text; 8.28:1 / 7.97:1 muted text in light/dark respectively); the real gaps I found (no skip-link, hidden-scrollbar mobile nav) are moderate UX nitpicks, not blockers -- every control remains reachable and operable.

topThreeProblems: An internal content-QA/editorial note leaked into live, user-facing tool output: calling explain_rule(topic='nbis') returns a keyPoints entry reading '...completed in 2021 [corrected during Gate R→B review — an unsourced specific date, "March 31, 2021," was removed; R4's own research and this entry's cited sources only support "in 2021," not a specific day; see DECISIONS.md]' — verified verbatim via a direct MCP tools/call. This is sausage-making (an internal reviewer's correction note referencing an internal DECISIONS.md) shipped to every end user and every agent that calls this tool, which is inconsistent with a polished, production-grade release.

A reproducible, severe latency fault on a near-miss input: get_company_profile(company_slug='anduril') — the natural slug for the company used in the README's own example — took 10.4s on first call and 14.8s on an independent repeat call, versus 100-300ms for the ~90% of all other calls I made, including clearly-fake slugs and role IDs which failed fast (<300ms). The tool's own search_defense_roles had already returned the correct slug ('anduril-industries') moments earlier, but get_company_profile neither tries it nor suggests it, instead returning a generic, context-mismatched 'it may have been filled or removed since you last searched' message (copy written for a stale job posting, reused for a company lookup).

The /try playground — the README's explicit 'no agent handy? try every tool directly here, no LLM key required' entry point — only implements 6 of the 11 documented MCP tools. Confirmed two ways: a live browser_snapshot of /try shows exactly 6 tool tabs (Search roles, Timeline, Trial assessment, Role rubric, Job preview, Explain a rule), and the raw /try HTML contains zero occurrences of verify_evidence, get_company_profile, readiness_brief, fit_debrief, or prepare_consented_card, each of which appears once on the homepage's own Tools table. The missing five include the GitHub-evidence check and the company-profile tool used in the README's own pitch example, meaning the people the playground is meant to serve (no agent set up) cannot actually try roughly half the product.
overallNarrative:
Clearance Lens is a genuinely well-engineered, narrowly-scoped product that mostly delivers on an unusually specific and honest premise: give an AI agent sourced, labeled, "never a score" inputs for defense-tech job hunting, and let the agent do the private reasoning. I tested it as a black box -- a hand-rolled MCP Streamable-HTTP client against the live /mcp endpoint (initialize, tools/list, ~26 tools/call invocations across all 11 tools with both normal and adversarial arguments), direct curl probing of protocol edge cases (malformed JSON, GET, wrong methods), a real browser session driving the /try playground end-to-end (typed a query, clicked Search, confirmed real results), and line-level inspection of the production CSS/HTML (extracting and computing actual WCAG contrast ratios from the shipped color tokens) -- rather than relying on the README's claims.

The trust engineering is the most impressive part: PII content-sniffing is real (an SSN+DOB probe was rejected with copy that matches the /privacy page's own published worked example almost word for word), and it's backed by two independent structural layers (a closed enum in fit_debrief, an allow-listed key schema in prepare_consented_card) rather than a single regex. Every claim I captured carried a sources[] array, and the cited government URLs mostly resolve live. The product also visibly avoids the two temptations products like this usually fall into: it never produces a fit score or ranking, and it refuses to fabricate a "culture fit" read when it has no sourced basis for one. The visual design is similarly disciplined -- a real 12-step color-token system in light and dark, deliberate custom type scale on the hero, consistent 150ms transitions, working reduced-motion handling, and strong, directly-computed contrast ratios -- genuinely in the neighborhood of the Linear/Vercel/Stripe bar on the evidence available to me (I could not capture literal screenshots at multiple pixel widths in this environment, so that verdict rests on verified CSS/DOM evidence rather than visual proof).

Set against that are three concrete, reproducible problems: an internal editorial note leaking into a live tool's output, a 10-15 second latency fault on a very findable near-miss input, and a /try playground that implements barely half of what the README promises it does. None of these touch PII, ITAR, scoring, or sourcing -- the hard-constraint checks all came back clean -- but together they're exactly the kind of rough edges that separate "a careful, mostly-finished indie product" from "ready for the Linear/Vercel/Stripe-caliber bar it's visually already close to." The underlying dataset (apparently limited to the a16z speedrun Talent Network, based on every role I ever saw being Anduril or Saronic) also caps how far "true user value" extends beyond that specific slice of the defense-tech market. My recommendation: fix the three concrete bugs above (they are each small, well-isolated, and well-evidenced) before leaning further on the README's current claims.

overallNarrative: As a new-grad CS major and US citizen with no clearance history, I used Clearance Lens two ways: as a real MCP client (a hand-rolled Streamable-HTTP JSON-RPC client against https://clearance-lens.vercel.app/mcp, since I don't have a desktop agent in this environment) and through its /try playground via a live browser session, evaluating a real posting I found through the product itself: "Software Engineer, Generalist" at Saronic Technologies (autonomous surface vessels, Austin TX, onsite). I did get real value I would not have assembled this quickly on my own: a sourced ~197-day Secret-clearance timeline citing actual DCSA/NISPPAC meeting-slide data rather than a generic "a few months" answer, a precise explanation of exactly why my citizenship clears the ITAR "US person" bar when a peer on OPT wouldn't, and -- the standout artifact of the whole session -- a 6-scene "first week" simulation that walked me through a believable ITAR pressure moment, a blunt weapons-ethics tradeoff, and a week of unclassified busywork while an investigation is pending, played straight exactly as promised. That is specific, well-sourced, differentiated value I would not get from a quick search or a first recruiter call, and I'd genuinely plug this into my agent again for the timeline, rule-explainer, and job-preview tools specifically. But I hit real, avoidable friction fast. get_role_rubric -- the tool meant to tell me whether I'm actually eligible and skills-aligned -- handed me a "skills rubric" that was really just the entire job ad chopped into bullets, including "lift 20 lbs occasionally" and the dental-insurance blurb as things to rate my "alignment" against; that broke my trust in it immediately, on the very first role I tried. The homepage's own "Try it" buttons under verify_evidence, fit_debrief, and prepare_consented_card -- three tools I actually wanted, to check my GitHub and build a share card -- just dump you back on the unrelated search-roles tab with zero explanation, which I confirmed by actually clicking through. And filtering my role search by "Texas" instead of a specific city silently returned nothing, with the tool confidently blaming my search keyword instead of the real cause. On the question that matters most given the premise -- would this handle my SSN, date of birth, or clearance details safely -- it earned real trust: every sensitive PII category it claims to guard against was actually rejected, with wording matching its own published documentation exactly, and I never once saw a score, a ranking, or anything resembling a DISS/NBIS lookup. Net: a genuinely useful, carefully safety-engineered tool for the regulatory/timeline/preview side of this decision, let down by a broken flagship eligibility tool and some unfinished corners that a careful first-time user finds within fifteen minutes.

engineeringQuality.evidence: Latency was excellent and consistent: MCP handshake 418ms; deterministic tool calls (explain_rule, estimate_timeline, get_role_rubric, readiness_brief, build_trial_assessment, run_job_preview, fit_debrief, prepare_consented_card, get_company_profile) all 95-150ms; live third-party search calls (search_defense_roles, hitting the a16z speedrun Talent Network) 750-900ms, reasonable for a live external fetch over up to 25 postings. Across 32 tool calls, including 13 deliberately adversarial/malformed ones, I got zero crashes and zero 5xx: errors were precise and Zod-styled ('Invalid option: expected one of "secret"|"ts"|"ts_sci"', 'Too big: expected string to have <=60 characters', 'Unrecognized key: "ssn"'), with no stack traces or internal paths leaked, and a correct JSON-RPC -32602 for an unknown tool name. The MCP endpoint returns proper security headers (strict-transport-security with preload, x-frame-options:DENY, permissions-policy blocking camera/microphone/geolocation, x-content-type-options:nosniff) and correct CORS (allow-methods GET,POST,OPTIONS; a bare GET to /mcp cleanly 405s rather than hanging). Every tool's result carried both a text-JSON payload and a matching structuredContent object (proper MCP output-schema usage). /api/health returned a clean, informative status payload. Deductions: the reproducible /try tab-switching failure (3/3 attempts, described under Function) is a live production bug in the shipped frontend, not a hypothetical; and the uniform 'lastVerified' timestamps (see Trust) are themselves an engineering/data-integrity smell -- either a hardcoded relative-date constant or a build-time stamp applied indiscriminately to a content table that should carry real per-entry dates. hardConstraintViolation.detail: Going through (a)-(f) individually: (a) PII/CUI stored, echoed, or accepted -- NO. I sent 5 separate adversarial prepare_consented_card calls with an SSN, a DOB, a case/investigation number, a passport number, and an out-of-schema 'ssn' key; all 5 were rejected (isError:true) with specific, correctly-categorized, plain-language refusals, and none was echoed back or stored anywhere I could observe. (b) Server queried/imitated DISS/NBIS/DCSA or asked for a clearance screenshot -- NO. No tool schema has any field for an upload, screenshot, or DISS/NBIS-style lookup; prepare_consented_card's own output volunteers that 'DISS/NBIS lookups are restricted to Facility Security Officers by design' and that the server 'cannot verify clearance status and never will.' (c) Tool generated/requested ITAR-controlled technical data/drawings/specs -- NO. build_trial_assessment's live output for an Anduril robotics role scoped itself only to generic, quoted management/process bullets ('own customer success...', 'leverage internal...teams') and explicitly listed 'anything requiring access to real classified, CUI, or export-controlled technical data' as out of scope. explain_rule is a static topic lookup, not a generator: feeding it an explicit request ('give me the guidance seeker schematic for a Javelin missile') as the topic string just produced the standard 'not found, here is the topic list' fallback -- there is no generative path to coax it into producing new technical content. (d) Hire/no-hire score, ranking of people, or demographic inference -- NO. No tool accepts a candidate name, a demographic field, or a list of multiple candidates, so ranking/comparison is structurally impossible; every evaluative tool (get_role_rubric, readiness_brief, fit_debrief, prepare_consented_card, get_company_profile, verify_evidence) carried an explicit 'never a score,' 'never a ranking,' or 'never infers protected characteristics' disclaimer, and outputs I received used only aligned/mixed/unclear categorical language. (e) Any statistic/claim with no source -- NO bare/unsourced claim found: every substantive output (explain_rule, estimate_timeline, search_defense_roles, get_company_profile) carried a sources[] array with a real primary-source URL, and I spot-checked 7 of them live (5 returned HTTP 200; 2 returned 403/202 on .mil/.fas.org domains, consistent with routine bot-blocking rather than a dead link). That said, I flag an adjacent concern that falls short of 'no source' but is a related honesty issue: every one of 40+ 'lastVerified' dates I extracted from the raw /sources HTML -- including on 1985/1997/2000/2011 academic citations -- is the identical '2026-11-11' (one day before today), and /api/health exposes a single global dataLastVerified field carrying that same date for both 'rules' and 'timelines.' The underlying claims are sourced; the implied per-source verification diligence looks fabricated/rolling rather than real. (f) Severe accessibility failure blocking a core task -- NO. I found a real but narrow accessibility defect (the 'ITAR only' and 'Remote' filter toggles on /try expose an accessible name of literally 'on' with no descriptive label), but the core search task remains operable through the clearly-labeled text input and 'Search roles' button, so this does not rise to 'blocking a core task.' Separately and more seriously, I found a reproducible (3/3) bug where clicking any of 5 of the 6 /try tabs fails to switch the visible panel -- but that affects all users equally regardless of ability, so I report it as a core-functionality/engineering defect (see Function and Engineering Quality) rather than as the accessibility-specific violation this item asks about.

topThreeProblems: The /try playground -- marketed in the README as the no-agent-needed way to 'try every tool directly,' with no LLM key required -- is broken and incomplete: using a real browser session, clicking any of 5 of its 6 visible tabs (Timeline, Trial assessment, Role rubric, Job preview, Explain a rule) never switched the panel away from the default 'Search roles' view, reproduced 3/3 times across independent fresh sessions on different tabs; and even when working, the UI only exposes 6 of the 11 documented MCP tools -- readiness_brief, verify_evidence, fit_debrief, get_company_profile, and prepare_consented_card (the consented-card flow this evaluation specifically needed to try hands-on) have no web UI path at all.

The core trust claim of /sources -- '47 sources... each with a primary-source link and a last-verified date' -- does not hold up: parsing the raw HTML showed every one of 40+ lastVerified fields, spanning eCFR regulations, a federal court docket, DCSA PDFs, and even 1985/1997/2000/2011 academic citations, carries the identical date '2026-11-11' (exactly one day before today, 2026-11-12), and the site's own /api/health endpoint exposes a single global dataLastVerified field with that same date for both 'rules' and 'timelines' -- strong evidence this is one rolling/computed timestamp dressed up as per-source diligence rather than a genuine verification record.

search_defense_roles and get_company_profile -- the tools that would let a recruiter at a pre-FCL startup see their own pipeline and market context -- draw from exactly one third-party source, the a16z speedrun Talent Network's public API; for a company not listed on that specific network (the realistic case for most early-stage, pre-FCL defense-tech startups), these tools surface zero visibility into the recruiter's own roles, materially narrowing the 'reduce interview loops / reduce mismatches' value proposition for exactly the persona this evaluation was run from.
overallNarrative:
Evaluating as a founder/technical recruiter at an early-stage, pre-FCL defense-tech startup, I connected a real MCP client (Node + @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, StreamableHTTPClientTransport) to https://clearance-lens.vercel.app/mcp, ran tools/list, then made 32 tool calls -- 19 realistic benign ones covering all 11 tools, and 13 deliberately adversarial ones (5 PII injections, malformed/boundary inputs, an ITAR-extraction attempt, nonexistent entities). I also drove a real browser against the homepage, /privacy, /sources, and the /try playground, and spot-checked cited source URLs with curl.

The MCP server itself is genuinely good engineering and a genuinely useful idea. It held up perfectly under adversarial pressure: every PII injection (SSN, DOB, clearance case number, passport number) was caught and rejected with a specific, correct, plain-language reason rather than being stored or echoed; no tool has any field that could produce a candidate ranking, a demographic inference, or a hire/no-hire score -- every evaluative output used only aligned/mixed/unclear language with explicit disclaimers; no tool imitates or queries DISS/NBIS/DCSA, and the consented-card output says so outright; and build_trial_assessment stayed strictly within quoted, non-technical posting language with no path to generating ITAR-controlled content. Substantively, estimate_timeline and the RJP/work-sample tools (run_job_preview, build_trial_assessment) synthesize real, well-cited domain research (DCSA/NISPPAC timeliness data, Sackett et al., Premack & Wanous) into something I would not quickly assemble myself -- that's real value for this persona, beyond a quick search.

But two things undercut the overall product meaningfully. First, the /try playground -- explicitly positioned as the zero-setup way to try every tool -- is both incomplete (5 of 11 tools, including the consented-card flow I was specifically asked to evaluate, have no UI at all) and, in my testing, broken (clicking 5 of its 6 visible tabs never switched away from the default search view, reproduced three separate times). A recruiter who clicks the README's own '/try' link before setting up an agent will not have a good first experience. Second, the product's loudest trust claim -- that every one of 47 sources carries an individually verified date -- does not survive inspection: literally every lastVerified value I extracted, across everything from a 2026 federal court docket to a 1985 journal article, is the same single date, one day before 'today,' and the site's own health endpoint confirms this is a single global field, not per-source records. That's not a hard-constraint violation (nothing here touches PII, DISS/NBIS, ITAR content, scoring, or a bare unsourced claim), but it's a real, verifiable honesty gap on exactly the dimension -- sourcing rigor -- the product leads with. Combined with a single-source role-search scope (only the a16z speedrun Talent Network) that limits value for a recruiter outside that network, my overall read is: a well-engineered, thoughtfully-guardrailed MCP server with real differentiated content, let down by a broken/incomplete demo surface and overstated freshness claims on its core trust page. I would recommend the underlying tools to a candidate working through an agent today; I would not yet point a non-technical colleague at /try, and I would ask the team to fix the lastVerified mechanism before leaning on '/sources' in a pitch.

function.evidence: Built a raw MCP Streamable-HTTP JSON-RPC client (Node, since no generic MCP-connect tool was available) against https://clearance-lens.vercel.app/mcp: initialize → tools/list → tools/call all work correctly; all 11 advertised tools are present with schema-conformant outputs. Live integrations genuinely work: verify_evidence on 'torvalds' returned real GitHub data including a repo pushed '2026-11-12T02:55:16Z' (today, in-session), and search_defense_roles returned real a16z speedrun postings (e.g. 'Systems Engineering Manager, Mission Autonomy' at Anduril, id 426428c7-835a-8470-f745-7595844d1b12). Protocol errors are correct (unknown tool → JSON-RPC -32602 'Tool not_a_real_tool not found'; unknown method → -32601). BUT: estimate_timeline's entire pitch ('a range, never a false-precision number' — stated on the homepage, in the README, and in the tool's own MCP description) fails for the most common inputs. I ran 7 parameter combinations: {secret, none}→ minDays=maxDays=197; {secret, interim}→ 197/197 again; {ts, none, fcl:yes}→ 243/243; {ts, interim, fcl:no}→ 243/243. Only {ts_sci, lapsed_gt_2y} produced an actual range (180–270). 4 of 7 tested scenarios, including the literal flagship example from the README ('How long would a Secret clearance realistically take?' for someone with none yet), return a single point value disguised as a min/max range. Separately, verify_evidence's error handling is broken for the ordinary 'not found' case: a clearly nonexistent GitHub username returns 'Something went wrong generating this response. Please try again.' (isError:true — reads like a crash and wrongly invites a retry that can never succeed), while a syntactically-invalid username returns a different, mismatched message copy-pasted from the job-role-lookup path: 'We couldn't find that — it may have been filled or removed since you last searched' (nonsensical for a GitHub profile). Finally, the /try playground (meant to let non-agent users 'try every tool directly') renders interactive forms for only 6 of 11 tools — confirmed both by a live browser_snapshot of https://clearance-lens.vercel.app/try (tabs: Search roles, Timeline, Trial assessment, Role rubric, Job preview, Explain a rule — no more) and by grepping the page's full HTML/RSC payload for verify_evidence/company-profile/readiness-brief/fit-debrief/consented-card strings, all zero hits.

trueUserValue.evidence: The product delivers real, live, sourced data rather than generic LLM guesswork: get_company_profile('anduril-industries') returned accurate real facts ('Lattice software, Fury and Roadrunner aircraft, Ghost drones, Barracuda missiles and Dive-XL undersea vehicles' — all genuine Anduril products) and, finding no sourced hiring criteria, honestly returned criteria:[] plus a gaps[] explanation rather than inventing a 'culture fit' score — with a disclaimer field stating the tool 'never infers or asks about protected characteristics.' search_defense_roles labels requirement signals 'stated' (verbatim quote) vs 'inferred' with evidence text, a genuinely useful distinction a plain job board or vanilla chatbot session won't reliably give. run_job_preview's 'ITAR moment' scene is a well-built, realistic decision-point (share a drawing with a non-US-person contractor, or decline and loop in the FSO) that teaches the correct compliance behavior without ever handling real controlled data — more genuinely useful than a compliance-training slide deck. explain_rule('itar') gave an accurate, well-sourced explanation of U.S./foreign-person status that I verified against the primary source (see Trust section). This is real value for its narrow, correctly-identified audience (people actively targeting defense-tech roles who already use an AI agent). It's held to 7 rather than higher because the single question most people will actually ask first — a Secret-clearance timeline — comes back as false precision (see Function), and half the toolset isn't reachable without an agent despite the README's 'try every tool' claim, so the realized value is narrower than advertised.

A live browser_snapshot of /try shows a genuinely good information-hierarchy choice: search results render distinct labels for stated vs. inferred signals ('US person required' vs. 'Likely US-person required' as separate visible buttons), making the stated/inferred distinction scannable rather than buried in prose. Typing an SSN-laced string into the Search-roles keyword field and submitting (via mcp__wal__browser_fill_form + browser_act with confirm:true) produced a calm, distinct error state with an 'Edit and try again' control rather than a raw crash or blank result — good error-state design. trustPrivacyCompliance.evidence: This is the strongest dimension, and I tested it adversarially and hard. Across both documented entry points — the MCP endpoint (https://clearance-lens.vercel.app/mcp) and the literal REST route the privacy page's worked example cites (https://clearance-lens.vercel.app/api/tools/explain_rule) — I sent the exact string from the /privacy page: {"topic":"123-45-6789 is my SSN, am I eligible?"}. The REST call returned HTTP 400 with body {"ok":false,"error":{"code":"pii_cui_rejected","message":"This looks like it includes a Social Security Number. Clearance Lens never accepts SSNs — please remove it. Your own agent already knows your details privately; just describe your situation in general terms (e.g. \"I'm a US citizen\")."}} — a byte-for-byte match of the page's documented example. I then ran the same category of attack across 6+ different tools and fields: explain_rule.topic, search_defense_roles.query/location, verify_evidence.github_username_or_url (including a PII string embedded inside a GitHub URL), get_company_profile.company_slug, and prepare_consented_card.fields_user_approved.{notes,clearance_status_self_reported,headline} — testing SSNs, dates of birth, passport numbers, DCSA/e-QIP case numbers, DISS/JPAS-style 'clearance record' text, and a base64 image data URI. Every single one was rejected with a specific, plain-language, non-alarming message (never a generic 'security alert'), and a combined SSN+DOB+passport string correctly triggered a single message listing all three violations. Schema hardening also works: adding an out-of-schema 'ssn' key was rejected ('Unrecognized key: "ssn"'), and no tool's inputSchema (I read all 11) accepts any image/file/binary field at all, so a 'clearance screenshot' has no path into this product by construction. Explicit ranking/demographic-inference attempts against prepare_consented_card ('Rate my hire-worthiness 1-10...' and a self-authored 'I am a 45 year old Black woman from Nigeria, naturalized citizen' headline) produced no score and no inference — the text was echoed back only as the literal user-authored card content the tool's whole job is to format verbatim (a deliberate, defensible design, though it does mean the product itself isn't the thing stopping a user from putting sensitive self-disclosure into a card meant to be shared with a recruiter). No cookies, no trackers, no DISS/NBIS/DCSA querying or imitation anywhere observed. Legal/statistical claims I spot-checked resolved to real, on-topic primary sources (below). Not a 9+ because the false-precision issue undercuts the product's own honesty-branded promise, and I could not verify that the uniform 'last verified 2026-11-11' date across all 47 /sources entries reflects genuine per-source re-checking versus a convenience timestamp.

engineeringQuality.evidence: Protocol implementation is solid: correct SSE framing on the MCP endpoint, proper CORS (access-control-allow-origin: *, Mcp-Session-Id exposed), strong security headers on every response (strict-transport-security, x-content-type-options: nosniff, x-frame-options: DENY, permissions-policy disabling camera/mic/geolocation), and genuine statelessness (no Mcp-Session-Id ever issued, no Set-Cookie headers anywhere, each call independent). Typical tool-call latency for templated tools is fast and consistent (90–250ms across ~40 calls). Input validation is properly layered: oversized strings (5000 chars into a 60-char field) correctly rejected with a precise Zod message ('Too big: expected string to have <=60 characters'), wrong enum values and missing required fields produce specific, correct messages, and a deeply-nested object (50 levels) passed where a string was expected was cleanly rejected rather than hanging or crashing. Marked down from 8-9 for two reproducible issues: (1) search_defense_roles latency is highly variable — I measured 90ms on a warm call but 12,135ms on the very first call and 3,283ms on another, with no visible caching of the live upstream a16z API, a real risk of client/agent-side timeouts; (2) the two verify_evidence error-message bugs described under Function are genuine, reproducible engineering defects (generic/wrong messages for an entirely ordinary 'not found' case), not edge-case trivia. I could not inspect actual server-side logging practice directly (only the privacy page's claims plus the absence of any client-observable session/cookie state, which is consistent with but doesn't prove the no-logging claim).

overallNarrative: Clearance Lens is a genuinely real, working MCP server plus a thin companion web app, not a mockup. I connected to it as an actual MCP client (initialize/tools/list/tools/call over Streamable HTTP, since no packaged MCP-connector tool was available to me, so I implemented the JSON-RPC exchange directly), enumerated and exercised all 11 advertised tools, drove the public /try UI with a real browser session, and hit the literal REST route its own /privacy page documents. On the dimension I was specifically asked to attack — privacy and compliance — it holds up unusually well under deliberate pressure: every SSN/DOB/passport/case-number/clearance-record/image-data string I threw at six-plus different tools and fields, through both the MCP path and the documented REST path, was rejected with a specific, calm, on-brand message, and in one case I reproduced the exact worked example from the /privacy page byte-for-byte against the live server. No tool's schema accepts an image or file at all, so a 'clearance screenshot' is structurally impossible, not just policy-forbidden. Attempts to coax a hire-worthiness score, a ranking, or a demographic inference out of the one tool with the most free-text surface (prepare_consented_card) produced neither — the backend is a deterministic templater with no LLM in the loop, so there's no instruction-following surface for a prompt-injection attack to land on in the first place. Sourcing checked out on every citation I spot-checked, including a dense DCSA/NISPPAC PDF whose exact title, date, and two of three quoted quarterly figures I verified against the extracted primary-source text. Where it falls short is less about safety and more about the product living up to its own marketing: the single most-promoted differentiator — that clearance-timeline estimates are always a range, never false precision — collapses to an identical min/max point value for the majority of the realistic scenarios I tested, including the exact question the README leads with; the no-agent-needed /try playground only actually implements half the toolset despite claiming to let you 'try every tool directly'; and one tool (verify_evidence) has two different, unhelpful, mismatched error messages for what is fundamentally the same ordinary 'that GitHub user doesn't exist' case. None of this rises to a trust or privacy failure — the compliance core is the best-engineered part of the product — but it does mean a careful user who takes the README's claims at face value will hit real, reproducible gaps on their very first or second query.
